projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Ruth Marie Eddins was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Please spell your last name for me.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Okay. Ruth Marie Eddins, E-d-d-i-n-s.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay. And this is just like Wizard of Oz, Ruth. You just have to ignore the guy behind the curtain. Just talk to me.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Oh, to you. All right. [Chuckles]

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Forget the camera's even there.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Great. Well, I was wondering, Ruth, if you could tell us where you were as it--as it got late into the '30s, and--and war started in Europe. And the--the Japanese and the Chinese have been fighting. And where were you, and how did you feel about all that?

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Well, during--at that time, we knew about over in China and over in the Philippines, and what was going on. And over in Europe, about the war in Europe, and--but on this particular Sunday morning, we were at that my parents' house. And it came over the radio about--just about 11 o'clock, about noon. And I remembered my--our son was in the high chair, and my parents was all there. And my sister we said to--my husband said, "Oh, we gotta go get Thelma 'cause her girlfriends." One of girls who just got married, and there was three other boys from Caldwell had just gone--had just left San Francisco and had gone over to the Wake Islands to make air strips. And so this is how we started, and we then we found the girls. And then we told them about the day that the war had been declared. And so, of course, everybody was upset because we didn't--we were--we were young, and we had families. And so many of them--the first thing that happened there in Caldwell, a lot of the young fellows that was in the National Guards went right down and signed up, a lot of the our friends. And then my husband, since we had Jack, why, he didn't sign up. And so we had been talking about going to do defense work. I mean they were--it's on the radio. If you can help, do this and do that so. We decided to go to--down to Burbank. We had some friends down there. And Roy had said, "Bill, you should come down. Lockheed needs people." So then we decided to--Roy came up. And we all got together and packed up our things, left all of our material things at his folks, and then we got in our car and just put--we--our clothes that we needed and just essential things. And then we go down to Burbank. And then when we got to Burbank, why, then we decided the first thing we should do is--Roy said, "Now, you go to work with me, Bill, and--and sign up at the employment division." So then Bill went down the first day, and he signed up. And then he come back on the bus. And, of course, he got lost to coming back to Burbank 'cause he had go down through L.A. and from a small town Caldwell Idaho. Why, you weren't used to that and so. But, anyway, he got home in the evening. And so then he goes to work the following Monday. Then on the--after he had gone to work for a week, then I went down and put in my application to go to work at Lockheed. And so then I went--then I went. I asked for--I went asked for a swing shift, and we decided on the way down that if Bill would work days and I would work nights, we could have take Jackie. And we would in the mornings, he would go with the people in the neighborhood 'cause you would had (?U-rides?), and then I would go down in the afternoon and pick him up. And then he'd bring Jackie back to the house, and then I'd ride home with one of the neighbors. And this was how we work. And right at the first of the war there, right after--well, it was about two, three months. This, you know, it was from December 'till--and then the next summer, it was in the summertime. We went down there in--on--in '42, you know.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Were there a lot of signs of the war in--in California? Were there still like barrage balloons and anti-aircraft guns and things like that around or--

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Blackouts more and--and smudge pots.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Tell us about those.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Well, you had all up and down, specially in Burbank, you had all these smudge pots up and down the street. And then if there was any for alert--for alert system wide, they would burn these so that you couldn't see any lights. You had keep all the light out. So this is one thing down there, and so you close, of course, all your windows. And it get pretty warm down there, you know, at times. And so, yeah. And then at the plant, you want to know about the plant.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Well, when you go to work, like at night, we had the soldiers on top of the plant. That was up there at all times at night. People didn't see them, I mean at night. And then, of course, all the shutters and everything was closed. You know, as we was working and, and then--let's see in about. And, of course, you had security. I mean, you go went through with a badge because there were thousands of us was working there, you know. And--and so then--and that rationing and everything was going on. Now, in California, it was lot worse rationing than it was in Idaho because we was in contact with our families. Now, they seemed to have more things up there in Idaho than we had in California--gas rationing, tires rationing, and--and like your meat. During that time, now, I would get up after--I'd get up about 10 or 11 o'clock and go to the market, and we stood in line. And I'd stand in line 'till probably with Jack, 'till about one o'clock. And then we get enough meat for--we try to get enough for two days so you weren't doing that everyday. And then this was when the shipment comes in, they gave us what they had. Of course, you had sugar and--and all of this and your margarine. But you was--you made do with what you had with the sugar and this stuff. But it was like your essential thing like your meat and things that you had to stand in line for. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Why the change from Caldwell to Burbank?

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Completely.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Was there a, for lack of a better way to describe it, a cultural shock for you guys?

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Well, now, when you went to work at the plant, you didn't--you didn't do the things that you was doing at home. I mean because we were young, and we belonged to a different clubs and things like that. You'd--you'd went to dances when you got down there and you was working. Now, a lot of times--now, Bill worked six days a week. But a lot of times, I worked seven days a week because that was when--on the B-17s and the B-19s. And so you didn't have much time you just with your family. I mean, you didn't. You was more or less just with your friends, just immediate friends, that--that worked at the plant, and--and you just, like, maybe if you have a weekend off, you get together have a dinner or something like. But nothing, no social life really. Until later on, I mean, right at first like, why, you know, there wasn't--there wasn't any. We didn't have the material to really go to war right at that time. You know, when they--when they bombed Pearl Harbor. We had family over there in Pearl Harbor. When it was bombed, of course, you was worrying your family and everything. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: How about news? Was news important? Did it seem to have float pretty easily?

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Find out about things?

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Yeah. You knew pretty much what was going through the papers and the radio. That was the main thing. Yeah. We knew what was going on, and how bad it got. And then, of course, on the newsreel if you got to--when we went to a movie, these newsreels that they had at that time, then they brought you up to date on a lot of this that was going on overseas and everything. You was late getting that, but you knew what was really going on, how bad it was really. What they were really doing. That was really bad. Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Is there a particular one of those newsreels that stands out in your mind?

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Well, this was kind a--this was the--the death march. You know, that type of thing over in the Philippines, but that was bad. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: And in fact there was a lot of--anti-Japanese feelings if you will--

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Definitely.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: There's a lot of anger in America.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: You bet your life. Now, you take--they're in Caldwell. They had a--a there was brought a lot of the Japanese from California, and they have camps, concentration camps, up there. And when anytime they tell you that they were mistreated, they weren't. They had a camp. And they had barracks just like our soldiers had, barracks down in, like, a (?Fort Ord?) and Fort Lewis and like that. The barracks was that, and they were up there. They had their little gardens and everything. And you--the road wet down below. And you could look up there, and you could see them up there. And so that is--they weren't treated badly at all. I didn't--I don't think. And so, of course, I'm one that I don't think what they've done to some of our men and some of our boys that was overseas and so some (far) prisoners. I--I can't see why we owed them anything. I mean that's my own personal opinion.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay. Let's go back to the plant. Take a few minutes, and tell me what you did at the plant, what your job was, and how you did that.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: When I first went to work there, I went to work as a riveter and buck--buck the rivets. And--and then we had to learn to, like use your drill, to drill a hole, and put a rivet in there and buck it straight. Well, and I was there about a week, and then I was lucky enough I got to be an instructor. I was pretty good at it, doing what I did. And so then I instructed for about a month. And then they put me on the line and I helped a young fellow, and we put on the skins of the--and on six and seven bulkheads. So I did that. And then they needed somebody to put on the brackets for the Norden bombsight. And so then I started working on that. And what you did, you went to the jig, you got your jig out of the your tool shed, you have to have an okay to be able to mark--take this jig out, and then you put it up onto the bulkheads. And then you drill your hole and put your pins--drill your hole, put your pins in. And then -- then you would fix that so that this bracket for the Norden bombsight will have the pulleys in there. And so you fix that bracket on, had to be precise, because of the jig. And--and then when you got this in there, then you take this jig down. And then the idea of the--this bracket was--this Norden bombsight see was never, no. We--you're employee. Nobody. Only the Army had the Norden bombsight set in the plane. When it was finished and when it was going off the ground on the--the maneuver, that they were going on bombing, because I don't know. During that time, we knew what this Norden bombsight was made with the black widow spider that made the cross hairs in this bombsite. And then when you set that in by the navigator, why, then these pulleys and things that, what I was putting in the bracket or the pulleys, when they poke the button for the--to put the bomb, why, then the pulley would pull on these little brackets and then release the bomb. And that's how that the Norden bombsight work, and that's what I did. Then and, oh, several months, oh, about--it was about '44. It was that they moved this Section Six and Seven because they had took it to Bakersfield. Because that was when it was getting real bad overseas, you know, that--that we were having a-- [Interview interrupted by a phone call.]

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Hold on a second.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Oh, then.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay. You were talking about the--

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Well, they moved.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Moved the--

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Yeah. So they first--they brought up a several crews from Bakersfield. And so, now, I was given a crew of three men to learn, to read the blueprints, and--and my Section to do the bombsite bracket. And then each, like the skins--why, they had like three that went in that. And so--and then we took those and just run them through. We had them about a month. And then that's when they, they told us this, why they were moving the--the bomb. This Section Six and Seven for the bombsight because they--they didn't want the Japanese to get a hold of this. That was really our major thing with the B-17s. And let's see. Then after they moved that, then--then I went to work over on B-27s. And we pulled the--the tanks, the gas tanks, and put in the bulletproof gas tanks. And a girl that belongs to this chapter, she worked back in Omaha, Nebraska. And I didn't know this until she was telling what she did. She was one that made these bullet proof tanks back in Omaha, and we were putting them in the B-27s there in Lockheed, down in Burbank. And I thought that was quite interesting and--let's see. And then from B-27s and they--after they got those pulled and brought them all up to date, then my partner and I, we went out on the field and worked under the Army, under the inspection. And then that's when we put in the shims, if any, rivets, like, you know, like they made them crooked. Somebody would drill a hole crooked, or they didn't pull the skin like they should be pulled. Why, then we--my partner--we would take that rivet out, and then we would put a shim in. And then we would put it in with a larger rivet and--and put that in there so it made it. They say five times stronger than it was so that we knew that the whole bulkheads was strong condition. Yeah. So that's what I did.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: So you were actually out working--[Cough]. There in Army-Air Force inspection team. They go around and check all the things--

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: [Nods head]

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: You follow around, and they point something out?

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Yeah. They mark it, and this--you repair this, you know. They'll put the--their mark on it. Yeah. And so we had two of us was--two groups of us was out there. Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Were there a lot of mistakes or--

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: No, not too many. 'Cause you have an inspector up on the--on the floor all the time. Oh, you were watched. All that stuff had to be in precision, you know, you didn't. So you was real careful about it and they--now I'm talking about my department that I was in, what we were doing. And, why, we didn't--I don't think they found too many mistakes on the bulkheads and stuffs, you know, on the outer skins. Yeah. 'Cause those women, they did a good job, and there a lot of men was working there too. You know, there's a lot of men that couldn't go, young men. Yeah. But now, you take--when I was talking about moving the bulkheads, now, there was some men that resented women that worked there because, like with the crew that came in. For me, I had two men that quit on me, and they had to replace because they said they weren't gonna take instructions from--from a woman because they didn't think we knew what we was talking about. But the--the one--one of my men turned out to be the supervisor up there at Bakersfield so I know I did a good job. Yeah. Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Well, what I heard is that women tended to be much more careful and precise then.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Yeah. You did everything. And the women that was there--now at Lockheed, we were all around, I'd say all the way from 21 to, oh, 30. We were, you know, good. We were strong and, you know. And if you went to work there, you went there to work. You didn't go there just to play around, you know, so.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Did you ever think you got any special treatment for being a woman?

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: No, no. We didn't get any special treatment. 'Cause, no. No. I don't feel like we did. We did just like a man's job. I mean, that's what we were there for.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Well, the reverse of that is, instead of being treated special, you were treated worse?

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: [Laughs]

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Did you ever think you were treated differently or worse than the men that were working in the plant?

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: No. I'd--I'd--I don't think so. You--well, I felt like I could--I could do just exactly what a man could do. I mean, you know. I could--the same. Like your drillers, the drills, and the--the rivets, and stuff like that. The big-- 'cause I was dealing with a larger ones, not these little, tiny things, you know, so. Yeah. No. I felt I did a good job. When I see the B-17s now, I feel like that I'd done a real good job on them. And specially when I see these old war pictures and everything thing. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Well, while you were--you were doing this, did you guys ever consider that you're building these bombers that were bombing cities and things like that? Do you ever think about the impact of what you were doing on the war effort or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: You mean, did we feel bad, like, maybe, shooting, you know, like over there in Germany and things like that? No. I didn't feel bad about it. I mean you--you know. They declared war on us really. That's our attitude years ago was a lot different than like this now. We were all for our country. We felt that we owed our country and that we should protect our country. And now, these young people. I'm disappointed in a lot of the young people. If we had a war right here today I don't know how many would really--well, like we got today. Now, that we're in a about getting men to sign up for it. See. And--and they aren't running down there signing right up at the draft. They aren't, so.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: So this is a different kind of thing.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: It's a different world.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Well, we could talk about how I feel about it.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: [Chuckles] Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: I'm going to stay out of that.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay. So tell me a little bit about your--just kind of walk through your working day.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Well, let's see. I--well, you mean at the plant?

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Sure. Let's start--

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Well--

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Let's start with leaving your house.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Oh, first thing in the morning, I get up and take care of my son. And get him ready to--to go down to Lockheed, and then we go to Lockheed and then I sit out. Go to the parking lot, the certain spot, and then I'd go in the plant and we go in there. And we wore--we wore. We were dressed--now, we were dressed, like I was dressed in white coveralls. And--and we walked in there and then went up to our department. And then we went to work. And then at lunch time, we was wondering, we have a commissary. Where we all went for our dinner at night at the commissary and-- [Interview interrupted by a phone call.]

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: [Laughs]

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Now, we were--we were talking about your day. You kind of taking us up to lunch.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: In the commissary.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Yeah. Well, then we would go have our lunch and then we go back and then go to work and then. Oh, and in our break periods. This is why so many people my age or--well, they quit maybe 20 years ago, smoked. Because during that time that's one thing that--you would have a 10-minutes break smoke. They called it a smoke period, a 10-minute break. But they would let anybody smoke have this break, but if you didn't smoke, you didn't get your break. So, of course, you get cigarettes in the plants there, you know. That's one thing you couldn't get in the stores, but you could get them at--at the plant. You go there. So we all started going to get a pack of cigarettes and go out on to the commissary and lite a cigarette, and we--you just take a couple of puffs. And that's a--so you got your break. But then pretty soon, you got the habit. So that's where you get a lot of your elderly women smoking cigarettes. And it's hard to break because I was one of those smokers so I know how it is, but I--I haven't smoked for good many years. But that's one of things that's happened during the war that--oh, we talked about a lot about that. And then we go back to work, you know. And.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: When you talked about the noise level just a second there.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: That was off.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: That's really bad. Yeah. And, of course, you get use to it though. It's like anything else. And, of course, you didn't wear earplugs or anything like that, you know. And, no. It's--it was. But it wasn't that bad really, I mean. The things aren't nearly as bad as you might think. I mean you look back on them and say, "Boy, how did I put up with that?" But we were young. When you were young, things don't bother you like when you get older.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: So when you get older, when that happens--

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: [Laughs]

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Can you tell us what that's like?

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: [Laughs] Yeah. Now. Here old and, like, if you have some. Say you have a grandchildren that come in and are noisy, then you're not used to that kind of noise. Let alone what we went through during the war. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: See, you already talked a little bit about what you did when you weren't working.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Some of the ladies, I've heard, they had the--the ladies that weren't married and things, they had actually gone to dormitories and things like that for them they would to do that, or did they have to find their own housing or how did--

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Oh, yeah. You had to find your own housing. And it--it wasn't you didn't--you weren't looking for a nice apartment. You were lucky if you got a apartment with a bedroom in it, kitchen, you know. And this was the way it was then. It was like two rooms, and you--and so that's why. Well, it was no problem with us because we had Jack. And he had his, you know, his bed. And then we had our bed, and then we had the kitchen. And that's all. Yeah. Um-hum. No problem. And we'd, you know, you get--we're pretty friendly. There in Burbank, see, there were a lot of people worked at Lockheed. Right around your neighborhood. So you could get together with them. And like--like I say, when you all worked on a Sunday, why, you know, you didn't do then. But you'd have days off right, then get together. Yeah. But it wasn't any elaborate things, you know. Maybe, yeah. I mean it wasn't like after the war where you have barbecues and things like that. You didn't do things like that. You couldn't get the meat to have a barbecue. You know, you're lucky if you, you know, have a wiener roast. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: I think--take a couple of minutes and talk about President Roosevelt. And--and how important he was to the country?

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Oh, I'd tell you. He was--that was one of our, the best President we ever had. And I'd tell you. We all just idolized him. That's how we felt about Roosevelt. I mean iIt seems like he'd done everything like it should be done and helped the people. And--and even right in the depression time, right up to the wartime and, you know, that--I mean, all of this different things. During--during his time when he first come in the--it was really bad. Depression was bad. And--and no--there was no work. And when he came in, the first thing, like, he's--he had I had the CCC Camp, which was a wonderful thing for the young people. It is like the young people today don't have any--they don't have anything to do. Well, he had the CC Camps, and they have done a lot of work around--around our lakes and roads. And they build up lot of things, you know, and it--well, it made them better men out of them. You know, it took kids and made men out of them. And then after that, then he had the WPA, the older men. Then he started WPA where they could work. Instead of having a welfare, like we have now, we had WPA. The men could work, and--and they could make enough money that they could support a family. And you were the coming out the Depression, and anything was help then, you know. And people were used to going without. There was very few people that had enough that they could say they were well-to-do, or they could dress their children like they wanted, or they could feed their children like they want. It just wasn't there. You'd see a whole town that--that, you know. And so when they got all of these things, things started to brighten up. Then the next thing happened was when the war started. And then, of course, it was just like--it just. Everything started to boom--[Clears throat]--because they had to start making all these things. And so, and the young people that was in the CCC camp, most of them all sign up to go into the Army. And--and then the WPA, why, they would--they could get jobs for--in the service. I mean for the airplane plants and--and the shipyards and there was a lot of other plants that they, you know, like, even like the uniforms, people that could go to work in these shops and things like that. So that's started our--the good times. And that's why then everybody started getting cars and things like that.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: What about when President Roosevelt died?

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Oh, it was a sad thing. Everybody that was really a bad, bad. Everybody was so upset, you know. It was bad. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: And, you know, it happened as war was ending.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Yeah. And then--and then President Truman took over. Yeah. He was a great man too. I mean, some people didn't think he should of had the atomic bomb, that he used the atomic bomb, but I'm--I'm one of these people that I'm glad that he did because we could--we could have lost a lot of men, more men than we did. We lost a lot of men then. And I'd tell you we--the Japanese was a lot stronger than we ever thought they could ever be too, you know. They got pretty close several times, you know, that, so. And I really think that was right to--I mean you look back, and it was a catastrophe, losing all those people and everything. But something had to stop the war. We weren't it on the ground or with the ships. It was just one of those bad thing that happened. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Well, you think it's important that--that the country interested in what your generation did?

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Well, I'd--I'd tell you, I don't think the younger generation realized just what we did do, you know, for the country. They just think--well. So many of the women work now. And they--so they don't see that it was a complete change. Very few women worked at the time that--that the war started. And so then when the mothers had to take care of the house and--then and go to work too for the country, why, that--that's now, they're working for the money. Because they can't survive on one wage anymore, and which is bad. I--I don't--I would like to see it go back where the women would take care their children and just have one breadwinner, but I don't know that will ever happen because it's--it's out of hand out now.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: But you--you left your son to go work in this plant.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Even though you felt that way, why did you do that?

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Because I was working for the country. I mean, you know, I would have a purpose for my doing, but now, people are--the purpose they're using it for is to get a larger TV, a better car, and not worrying about the children. It's hard on the children. I think--I think the children needs to be supervised at home. I really do.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: 'Cause I know I have grandchildren that their mother and dad both work, but then the ones that are doing so well have their other grandparents that they take care of them while the parents work. They don't--they aren't just let go or--

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: So I think they need that family supervision really.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Let's see. I have another question, and I lost it.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: [Laughs]

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: What was I saying? Well, do you think that--that the war fundamentally changed the country? And how did the change the country? For the better? Or the worse?

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Well, it--it changed financially. It changed them for the better because they have more material things. Before the war, we didn't have so many material things, you know. And now, why, everybody's got--they got their cars, they got their TVs, and they got their computers and all of this. And before that, why, you went to school, and you have reading, writing, and arithmetic. And that was just about it, you know, and learn a little history and. But now, it's--everything is world wide. You know exactly what is going on all over the world now. And some of it, you look at some of the countries, it's bad. I mean look at India and what awful and how they're living and, you know. And some of these other countries and, of course, I don't--I hate, you know, in the Middle East, I wished we were never bothered with them--with them. They've been in war all these years, all forever, forever since the time of Christ. And now, we're in there and trying to tell them how to live. I don't believe that--they were doing--I mean they fought among themselves, but it isn't like it is anymore. Killing their people and everything. I don't--I don't like that.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: How would you summarized the wartime experience, and what it did for you or to you in your family?

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Well, I'd tell you--I'm--you're more conscious of how the United States is run. And you should take a part in that if you wanted--if you want. If you want things done, you should get out there and work for them. And I know when I was younger, I was really into the school, into legislature, and everything else but because I think the young people should participate more in all--their, like in their city things and their state, I think that should start participating in it more really.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay. And you think that the--that the having had the women go to work and the war industry that the--do you think that changed America? And in what way you would think that?

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Well, definitely a change because people were used to working, and they were used to getting a paycheck and everything. And so the women just kept right on working, you know. And then you turn right around. And then you have a Korean War right on top of the World War. Everything was getting back to normal in the '50s. And then you had the Korean War. And then you went along, and then--that people--some people you almost ignore the Korean War because you didn't think that was too important. But it was important, you know. And we had a lot of men over there, but it--we weren't--we weren't losing as many men and then so people weren't really conscious of how bad that was. And then we had the Cold War, you know. And had that could have been terrible, you know. And now, we got this other one, you know, so. I just think that I don't know where it's gonna end. It's not getting better.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Was there anything that--that you like to add about this experience for your family? For posterity stake? Is there something I didn't ask about?

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: For posterity? No. I'd thought a lot of the family and, why, they said, "[Gasps]--I didn't even you was Rosie the Riveter." You know, my neighbors, and stuff. They--a lot of people don't even realized what we've done during that time. Yeah. But--well, my boys, both--I felt that was good that they were in the Army. I--I like the draft. I'd like to see it come back. I'm not--not for war. But for the--now, you take my one boy. Like I say, he loved--he loved that Army. And he was stayed in it, you know. But then the other hated it, but he was--he needed that for the discipline of it. That and I think that is good for these young men, especially the discipline. Yeah. Cause at least he could take orders, you know. And I liked--I liked to see them when they really has some of these old sergeants that was really rough on them. Now, that's made me not a very good mother, but I thought it was good. [Laughs] When your mother and dad can't straighten them out, let the--let the Army straighten them out, you know. No. I--so, oh, I think our young people now, I know some of the young people that I know are doing excellent. They're going on to college, and I know I tried to tell some of them do your reading and--and make sure to make something of yourself. Don't give up, you know. And that's the main thing. I'd hate to see the kids--if the schools and things I think that they need. I need they--I think the schools should be a lot stricter than they are. I mean, you know, I think that's one thing that that's for our young people. I think they need to more supervision. And be a little rougher on them. I'm not--I'm one of these mothers that, they're like don't spare the rod, you'll spoil the child, so.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Did I leave anything out? Not that I can think of. Call that good then.

sp.speaker: Ruth Marie Eddins
sp.p: Oh. [Laughs]
